Radiant design is more than the absence of harm; it is the presence of thought-
ful, ethically-grounded design choices to ensure player well-being is not signifi-
cantly undermined while pursuing engaging experiences. True radiance implies

a constructive, positive orientation that may go beyond simply counteracting

manipulative techniques. This nuanced understanding is crucial as we advocate

for their broader adoption and exploration. A pattern could be neutral, nei-
ther dark nor particularly radiant. Radiant Patterns aim higher, representing a

conscious, positive design orientation focused on fostering healthier player-game

interactions, rather than merely existing as a negation of harmful practices. This

broader, more constructive view allows Radiant Patterns to be a guiding prin-
ciple for innovative game design, not just a corrective measure.

6.3 The Challenge to Evaluate Players Well-Being

Evaluating the well-being that these patterns may promote in players presents

significant challenges. [ 41 ] demonstrate that radiant patterns, in contrast to

deceptive ones, can raise awareness of ethical principles in digital games. How-
ever, evaluating the well-being that these patterns cause in players can be chal-
lenging. [ 41 ] work shows that radiant patterns, as opposed to deceptive ones, can

raise awareness of ethical precepts in digital games. However, it has not yet been

possible to investigate the real effects these patterns can have on well-being since

they need to be inserted into the context of a game to directly affect gameplay.

For gameplay to be complete, other factors affecting the player’s experience must

be considered, such as visual, sound, and graphic elements. Therefore, there is

a need to develop evaluation metrics that focus on radiant patterns in isolation

from other gameplay elements.

There is still no methodology to directly evaluate the well-being that these

patterns can cause in users. However, it is possible to assess aspects of intrinsic

motivation, such as autonomy, competence, and relatedness, which belong to

self-determination theory. This can be done mainly through instruments such

as the PENS scale [ 39 ] and the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI) [ 33 ]. As [ 8 ]

describes, positive intrinsic motivation and need satisfaction are fundamental to

Player Experience because they affect the gameplay moment and the broader

impact on player well-being. However, what results from the pattern itself or

the experience resulting from all the aspects present in gameplay? We invite

academia and the gaming industry to investigate methodologies that can deter-
mine whether motivation is genuinely positive due to its connection with the

game or the result of using radiant patterns.

6.4 A Radiant Pattern Repository

Radiant Patterns face the challenge of market acceptance, as deceptive pat-
terns are designed strategies that are already well established, widely used, and

profitable, despite being ethically inappropriate. They are employed, even when

Operationalizing Radiant Patterns 127

developers recognize their potential harm [ 1 ], which illustrates a complex indus-
try conflict. A next step in the evolution of Radiant Patterns would be to explore

how they can generate a return for the game industry, addressing the advantages

of Deceptive Patterns and making them more attractive to game developers.

This progress can be collaborative as Radiant patterns can be identified based

on players’ and researchers’ experiences with game mechanics. Applying the tem-
plate structure proposed in this work makes it possible to systematize the cre-
ation and documentation of these patterns. Thus, the Human-Computer Inter-
action (HCI) community and game developers can collaborate to identify and

refine new Radiant Patterns. This collaboration could lead to the development of

an open repository of standards, strengthening the creation of a gaming industry

guided by ethical principles and committed to promoting player well-being.

6.5 Study Limitations

Although a refined definition and a detailed structure for operationalization is

presented, no evaluations with players have yet been conducted to validate the

direct effects of Radiant Patterns on well-being. The difficulty in isolating the

effects of design patterns from other gameplay elements such as graphics, sound,

and narrative also compromises the accuracy of such assessments. Generalizing

these results may also be affected, as players’ perceptions of the patterns can

vary depending on their gaming experience, personal profiles, prior exposure to

games, and awareness of the consequences of digital design patterns.

Another important limitation concerns the practical adoption of these pat-
terns by the game industry. Although they offer an ethical alternative to decep-
tive patterns, Radiant Patterns have not yet demonstrated concrete commercial

viability. The adoption of such patterns may not offer game designers an imme-
diate return in terms of their key objectives, including engagement metrics and

financial performance.

7 Conclusion

This paper presents a refined definition of radiant patterns and a documentation

structure that serve as a template to help game developers as well researches to

identify and empirically validate radiant patterns for his operationalization. This

structure is exemplified through the implementation of a example of a refined

defined Radiant Pattern.

As a refined pattern built upon the Self-Determination Theory, we rein-
force that the basic psychological needs of players—autonomy, competence, and

relatedness—are not compromised by detrimental design decisions, preserving

current levels of need satisfaction as well avoiding adverse effects directly associ-
ated with psychological harm. In this work, the authors extend an invitation to

the Human-Computer Interaction community to contemplate the development

of ethical alternatives to deceptive patterns by employing our systematic tool to

collaboratively identify those alternatives.

Abstract. Digital games support well-being, yet dark patterns often
frustrate player needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Ra-

1 Introduction

Digital games have a dual nature. They can provide engaging and uplifting expe-
riences [13,11,16], offering relaxation, therapeutic outcomes, and social benefits
[29,39]. Yet, this potential is compromised when games are misused, including
excessive play linked to behavioral issues [33], toxicity in online communities [52],
and exploitative micro-transactions [32]. Such practices undermine well-being by
frustrating basic psychological needs [18] through dark or deceptive design pat-
terns [26,53], leading to negative emotional states, addictive behaviors [7], and
gaming disorder [31].
Dark Patterns (DPs)

informed decision-making [25], nudging users toward data surrender, unwanted

In games, DPs extend beyond isolated dialogs, embedding into progression, re-

2.1 Well-being and "Positive" Design Patterns

In contrast to manipulative strategies, positive computing positions well-being
as an explicit design objective rather than a byproduct of usability [8,9,42]. It
draws on multiple strands of psychological research to inform the design of sys-
tems that support human flourishing [9,43]. Among these, Self-Determination
Theory (SDT) provides a widely adopted and empirically robust framework for
understanding basic psychological needs. SDT identifies autonomy, competence,
and relatedness as fundamental needs [18,47], linking need satisfaction to in-
trinsic motivation and growth, and need frustration to diminished well-being
[47]. In design terms, these needs function as structural affordances: systems
cannot guarantee flourishing, but they can organize conditions that support or
undermine volition, efficacy, and connection [43].
Although Positive Computing and SDT provide a theoretical basis, restora-
tive design vocabularies remain fragmented. We compare three approaches –
Bright, Fair, and Radiant patterns – to clarify their scope and goals.
Bright patterns use persuasive design to support users’ genuine goals rather
than provider profit motives [49]. They reframe ambiguous persuasive techniques
to prioritize user welfare, for example through transparent onboarding or visual
countermeasures against scarcity cues. However, this approach introduces a nor-
mative tension between “nudging for good” and respecting autonomy, as steering
users toward desirable behaviors may risk ethical paternalism.
Fair patterns emphasize neutrality and regulatory compliance rather than
persuasion. They are defined as design solutions that restore fairness by providing
clear and timely information to facilitate informed decision-making [45]. Their
goal is to operationalize transparency and trust through mechanisms such as
layered notices and non-coercive defaults, with primary application in regulated
domains such as e-commerce and digital services.
Radiant patterns (RPs) are explicitly tailored to game design and grounded
in SDT. They aim to discourage addictive play and promote well-being by sup-
porting SDT basic psychological needs [21]. Unlike the broader applicability of
Bright or Fair patterns, RPs address specific gameplay structures. For example,
autonomy support involves making meaningful choices visible within the sys-
tem, while competence scaffolds foster skill-based mastery rather than artificial
retention loops [20]. This domain specificity allows RPs to target the intrinsic
quality of the experience, not only the transparency of the interface.
Because behavioral design inevitably shapes user action regardless of intent
[3], ethical concerns extend beyond whether persuasion is used and concern how

systems organize motivation. Many positive design initiatives risk focusing nar-
rowly on individual symptoms of harm while neglecting broader systemic causes
[46]. RPs address this by emphasizing the structural non-frustration of basic
psychological needs, establishing a pragmatic ethical baseline for game design
rather than prescribing idealized outcomes.
A further limitation across positive pattern approaches is the scarcity of
empirical validation compared to the iterative A/B testing commonly used to
optimize dark patterns. Without standardized definitions and shared criteria,
consistent implementation and evaluation remain difficult. Standardizing defi-
nitions and identification criteria provides the experimental units required for
large-scale testing. This framework establishes the consistent variables needed
for cumulative empirical research to assess impact on player experience.

2.2 Radiant Patterns

Radiant Patterns were introduced as an ethical, pattern-based approach to game
design in response to the prevalence of dark patterns and their negative impact
on player experience [38]. Rather than only cataloging harmful practices, this
work articulated recurring design solutions to guide developers toward ethically
grounded alternatives compatible with production constraints such as progres-
sion systems and monetization models. Initially, RPs were broadly defined as
patterns intended to support player well-being.
However, the emphasis on “preserving well-being” was considered too abstract
to guide consistent application, particularly since meaningful play often involves
tension and challenge [20]. The definition was therefore reframed to focus on the
non-frustration of psychological needs. Radiant Patterns are interaction patterns
intentionally implemented to ensure foundational player well-being is not signif-
icantly undermined. Specifically, RPs avoid decreasing autonomy, relatedness,
and competence. They are conscious design choices that minimize predictable
psychological harm and avoid patterns known to frustrate these needs, estab-
lishing ethical boundaries for player experience.
This shift from idealized flourishing to minimizing predictable harm demon-
strates how Radiant Patterns can coexist with commercial production goals. A
standardized template supports this by requiring explicit descriptions of how
each pattern avoids need frustration [20].
An initial set of six RPs previously outlined served as exemplars for this
approach [38,20]. While these patterns have been applied in reflective design
artifacts [21], the methodology for expanding this set remains underdeveloped.
The existing documentation template supports the recording of known patterns
but offers little guidance on the identification or derivation of new ones. Conse-
quently, the extension of the RP library has relied heavily on ad-hoc authorial
judgment, limiting its transferability to the broader research community [20].
This methodological gap compounds the empirical limitation identified in the
previous section. Without a structured process to generate and standardize new
patterns, the lexicon of Radiant Patterns remains too small and inconsistent
to support rigorous A/B testing against dark patterns. Therefore, the primary

tablishing a collaborative infrastructure and a structured methodology for the
identification, refinement, and validation of Games Radiant Patterns.

4.2 Refined RPs Framework Established a Shared Lexicon

Through a deductive thematic analysis of the workshop transcripts cross-referenced
with the refinement sessions we identified recurring criteria that let to a restruc-
tured RP framework, including revised titles, new levels, and template adjust-
ments.

Establishing How to Name a Radiant Pattern Discussion sessions revealed
that original titles were often too narrow or lacked alignment with the functional
depth of the patterns. Analysis of the lexical shifts produced four pragmatic
naming rules to guide future expansion:
1. Functional Abstraction : Use terms that describe the interaction state
rather than specific menus, labels, or literal UI elements or actions.
2. Generic Classification : Replace specific elements with broader functional
categories to ensure cross-platform neutrality.
3. Outcome Orientation : Focus the title on the systemic or psychological
result of the interaction rather than the specific object or mechanic involved.
4. Relational Characterization : Define the system’s active response to the
player’s status or skill rather than using static comparative descriptors.
These rules were applied to connect the titles of the baseline set of RPs
directly to their functional descriptions while providing a scalable protocol for
future repository expansion. The resultant changes were:
RP1 - Free Exit changes to Open Gate : The original title emphasized free-
dom to leave but did not convey progress preservation. The revised name
highlights both autonomy and progress security, adopting Open Gate as
a metaphor for seamless exit and return without cost.

RP2 - Free Pet Care changes to Companion : The term pet was too narrow
to cover the variety of companions in games. Companion broadens the
scope to include animal, human, technological, or symbolic entities with
decorative, narrative, or functional roles.
RP3 - Item Evolution changes to Progression : The original name restricted
the pattern to items. It was reframed to emphasize perceived progress
and achievement, decoupling it from exclusive item-based mechanics.
RP4 - World Creation changes to Creative Suite : The initial title centered
on world-building and did not reflect the range of creative experiences
in games. Creative Suite broadly encompasses player-generated content
such as customization, level design, system creation, and worldbuilding.
RP5 - Color Hint changes to Visual Support : Hint risked being interpreted
as tutorial guidance rather than gameplay affordances. Visual Support
broadens the scope beyond color cues and better reflects its role in miti-
gating visually blocking elements.
RP6 - Different Difficulty changes to Adaptive Challenge : The original
name suggested only player-controlled difficulty adjustments. The revised
title captures both manual adjustments and adaptive responses to differ-
ent player profiles and play styles.
By introducing these rules and applying them to the baseline RP set, we
promote clearer pattern identification without restricting patterns to specific
contexts, enabling expansion across settings. This supports future contextual
variants while preventing ambiguity that could hinder practical application.

Defining Hierarchical Scaling and Contextual Variants for RPs Discus-
sion revealed that original RPs failed to account for genre-specific constraints,
platform limitations, or player profiles. Contextual differences, such as the transi-
tion from single-player to multiplayer, are not isolated exceptions but structural
adaptations required to maintain the pattern’s efficacy. By analyzing these re-
quirements, we established two pragmatic rules for framework expansion:
1. Progressive Requirement Scaling : Structure pattern application into
hierarchical tiers, each representing increasing psychological need satisfaction
from a baseline of non-frustration.
2. Environment-Based Subclassing : Define structural variants that adapt
universal levels to specific gameplay contexts (e.g., genre, mode, platform)
without changing core logic.
These rules allow a more precise integration across varied RP titles. For
instance, the core mechanic of Companion requires different implementations
for decorative mascots in The Sims compared to combat partners in World of
Warcraft . Similarly, Creative Suite spans a broad design space—from aesthetic
customization to complex scenario sharing—that cannot be addressed by a single
description without losing developer utility.

Following progressive scaling, patterns are organized into universal applica-
tion levels. Level L1 establishes the ethical floor of non-frustration. While L1
represents standard practice, i.e., its inclusion in the framework identifies it as a
necessary boundary against deceptive monetization or retention tactics, L2 and
L3 progressively enhance need satisfaction. For example, Open Gate includes
L1 – Safety (automatic progress saving), L2 – Autonomy (intentional stopping),
and L3 – Competence (visual feedback reinforcing achievement).
The use of environment-based subclassing through variants ensures extensi-
bility. This dual structure allows practitioners to add contextual implementations
to the RP catalog while preserving each pattern’s conceptual identity.

An Updated Radiant Pattern Framework Workshop evaluations and re-
finement sessions confirmed that original pattern descriptions lacked the struc-
tural rigor required for industry application. The primary failure involved the
conflation of developer goals with player outcomes, which obscured how specific
design choices support ethical objectives. Furthermore, the absence of explicit
dimensions like genre or platform prevented the framework from capturing the
structural adaptations necessary for diverse play environments. Table 3 presents
the resulting template. This systematic structure reorganizes the Radiant Pat-
tern Framework, ensuring that every RP added to the catalog supports consistent
application and future extensibility without fragmenting conceptual integrity.
To ensure scalability of the RP framework, we defined four pragmatic rules
for the RP template:
1. Goal–Outcome Decoupling : Separate developers’ technical goals from

Player Problems (the experiential goals or need frustrations addressed).
2. Multi-Dimensional Scoping : Specify target actors and context to avoid
vague terminology and support diverse settings.
3. Invariant–Variant Duality : Define core properties (Invariants) that must
hold across adaptations to preserve identity, regardless of the Variant.
4. Traceable Need Satisfaction : Map each solution to hierarchical design
levels (L1–L3) to validate radiance through structural criteria.

5 A Catalog of Games Radiant Patterns

The Radiant Patterns Catalog 
6 
is a structured knowledge system designed to
bridge player well-being research and game development practice. It operational-
izes the multidimensional framework of Universal Levels and Contextual Vari-
ants derived from our refinement sessions. The platform is organized around
context-driven filters that allow practitioners and researchers to query patterns
according to developer goals and player needs, directly reflecting Phase I findings
on genre specificity and application context. The system distinguishes between
Finalized RPs – those validated through formal verification – and Candidate
RPs, which are undergoing co-creation. This separation enables transparency re-
garding pattern maturity while allowing users to choose between peer-validated
standards and experimental alternatives. Filters include variant-based con-
texts (e.g., Single-Player, Multiplayer) and development goals (e.g., preserving
progress, managing companions), all within the boundaries of the RP framework.
A core contribution of the platform is its tiered visualization of pattern levels,
translating abstract psychological principles into concrete design examples. Each
pattern presents its Universal Application Levels (L1, L2, L3) alongside a visual
carousel of real-world game instances. These examples, combined with textual
explanations, function as a semiotic bridge that illustrates how an RP manifests
across levels without requiring deep SDT expertise.
To ensure scalability, the platform includes a collaboration module en-
abling repository expansion. It supports two entry types: structured submissions ,
where contributors propose new patterns or variants using the RP template
vocabulary; and problem-based contributions , which document recurring design
problems requiring ethical alternatives. All submissions are flagged as Candi-
dates and remain visible but distinct from validated RPs until reviewed through
the governance process, preserving transparency while maintaining reliability.
To safeguard integrity, we propose a governance model in which community-
proposed RPs undergo a formal verification protocol modeled after the collabo-
rative workshops described in this paper. Sessions involving both academic and
industry specialists assess submissions against defined RP Invariants. Rather
than binary acceptance, proposals return to contributors for iterative refine-
ment, ensuring that candidate patterns remain accessible while being polished
into finalized standards. We invite volunteers from academia and industry to
participate as reviewers. Although reliance on a self-selected community may
introduce selection bias or uneven SDT expertise, the documentation template
serves as the primary objective check. By requiring mechanics to be mapped to
specific needs, it reduces the risk of subjective gatekeeping.

6 Discussion: Radiant Patterns and Industry Practice

The proposed Radiant Pattern framework provides a structured foundation for
both game developers and researchers to recognize positive practices that align
with developer goals while also analyses their impact on player’s well-being.
Specifically, for game developers, the framework helps clarify the distinction
between dark and radiant patterns and demonstrates how adopting radiant
approaches can positively impact players, fostering more ethical and player-
centered experiences while avoiding negative consequences. For game researchers,
the framework offers a template to identify emerging radiant practices, analyze
their impact on players, and advance researches focused on ethical game design.
By cross-referencing discussions from the collaborative workshop and refine-
ment sessions, we were able to refine what makes a Radiant Pattern “radiant.”
As participants initially struggled to understand how RPs could positively affect
players on the original set of patterns, the refinement became essential to explic-
itly show their potential impact on players’ basic psychological needs and clarify
which development goals they support. This refinement enables game developers
to more directly adopt those pattern due to his alignment with development goals
while ensuring foundational player well-being, as articulated in the operational
definition of Radiant Patterns [20]. We clarify that L1 is a defensive baseline
rather than an aspirational peak. It represents ’not-Dark’ design, serving as the
essential technical foundation upon which L2 and L3 build active support for
player flourishing, using suitable mechanics in the game industry.
Unlike DPs, which are engineered for profit extraction through behavioral
exploitation, RPs provide a path for sustainable player engagement grounded
in need satisfaction rather than psychological coercion. We recognize that while
certain DPs may generate short-term revenue gains, RPs offer a framework for
sustainable player engagement. Financial success from DPs does not justify their
use nor does it prevent the development of better standards. Providing alterna-
tives such as the RPs establishes a technical basis for a more responsible industry,
so short-term gains do not necessarily dictate the future of player experience.
RPs provide developers with an actionable standard that respects player agency
without conflicting with the inherent tensions and challenges required for engag-
ing gameplay.
As we created new pattern titles and established universal levels of applica-
tion alongside context-specific variants, we evolved the pattern set from a gen-
eralized formulations to specific applications, thereby expanding its relevance
across different genres and player’s profiles. This evolution was made possible by
broadening the discussion beyond the initial authors [20] to a specialized panel
with diverse academic backgrounds and development practices. This panel re-
fined the logic and, yet nine participants offer a focused expert perspective rather
than a global industry consensus, they enriched the process with practical ex-
amples and developer expertise. The new titles, variants, and levels produced
a more actionable set of Radiant Patterns while maintaining the qualities that
define them as such. Central to this evolution is the development of a standard-
ized lexicon that bridges the communication gap between research and practice,

The autoethnography identified RPs in released games, confirming their real-
world presence. This analysis serves as a discovery method, though validating the
framework’s use during active development remains a future requirement. Just
as DPs were identified through critical observation of manipulative practices in
the game industry[56], analyzing game structures through the RPs framework
allowed researchers to identify design practices that either avoid needs frustration
or support the fulfillment of basic psychological needs. The structural evolution
of the RP framework from generalized formulations to context-specific variants
addresses a core challenge in player experience research which is the inability to
account for unique, genre-specific interactions [28].
By establishing universal levels alongside these variants, the Radiant Pat-
terns framework a contextually-specific approach, recognizing that the ethical
impact of a mechanic is grounded in the unique characteristics of its gameplay
environment[3]. It is important to clarify that the Universal Levels (L1-L3) are
intended as a methodological baseline rather than a claim of universal experi-
ence. While the experiential reality of a patterns varies wildly between genres,
such as the difference between competence in a sandbox and a soulslike, the re-
quirement to not frustrate basic psychological needs remains the common ethical
denominator. Hence, the RP variants allow the lexicon to remain stable while
respecting these diverse contextual boundaries identified in the literature.
The common lexicon aims to offer a systematic alternative to rapid-response
research triggered by technology panics [41]. Yet, a shared vocabulary is a tool
for interaction design, not a solution for all ethical challenges. Systemic issues
such as game worker welfare, harassment, and online toxicity require regulatory
and cultural interventions that lie beyond the scope of interaction design [27].
Besides, identifying these new mechanics through autoethnography does not
automatically qualify them as Radiant Patterns. This is why they are referred
on findings as candidate RPs. Identifying an RP requires evidence of recurrence,
which establishes it as a pattern[2], as well as discussion and coherence with the
components defined by the framework. This distinction creates a logical need for
the Radiant Patterns Catalog (Section 5). Because a single autoethnographic
instance cannot confirm a pattern, and a 10-hour sample may not capture the
full systemic depth of complex titles, the Catalog serves as a filter where these
initial observations are flagged for further verification. The ’candidate’ ideas
are subjected to a verification protocol. This ensures that only those designs
proven to be recurring and ethically sound are finalized, transforming subjective
observations into community-validated design knowledge. Expert observation
may result in false positives, reinforcing the need for the Catalog’s collaborative
verification protocol in which the practical application of these patterns can be
observed, analyzed, and discussed collectively.
Current constraints include the absence of longitudinal testing. Establishing
the RP framework and catalog provides the technical foundation needed to move
toward support for positive impact. Yet, the RPs Catalog is the digital infrastruc-

7 Final Remarks

This work evolves the RP framework by shifting focus to the structural non-
frustration of basic psychological needs through a refined lexicon, tiered levels,
and standardized templates. These components establish a system to connect
ethical research with game development practice. While this version lacks longi-
tudinal data, relies on a small expert-centric sample, and excludes systemic issues
like worker welfare or online toxicity, it establishes the technical foundation for
future industry-led verification.
Future work focuses on testing long-term impact, expanding the relatedness
dimension based on observed dialogue-driven instances, and implementing the
collaborative verification protocol to transition candidate patterns into finalized
standards. By providing this structure, the framework offers a technical path
for the industry to move beyond identifying dark patterns toward the active
co-creation of design cultures centered on player well-being
